extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in U.S. patent law (law students, practitioners, policy makers, and informed public)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of the legal standards and criteria used in Mayo Collaborative Services v. Prometheus Labs. for determining patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101, especially for diagnostic methods and laws of nature. Useful for understanding how courts and the USPTO assess claims that involve natural phenomena or correlations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 101 patent-eligibility / natural law exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A discovery of a new natural phenomenon (or a law of Nature) is not by itself patentable; claims that are directed to such natural laws or phenomena do not meet the patent-eligible subject matter criterion under 35 U.S.C. §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Wikipedia article summarizes Mayo's basic idea: although discovery of a natural phenomenon may satisfy non-obviousness, patent claims that either wholly pre-empt the natural phenomenon or add no additional 'inventive concept' to this discovery fail §101. The Court called the correlation between metabolites and efficacy/toxicity an unpatentable 'natural law.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patent-eligible, a claim that involves a law of nature must include an 'inventive concept' — something more than the natural law itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court in Mayo held that the claimed method 'does not add an inventive concept to the application of the natural laws.' The Court emphasized that merely applying a natural law using well-known, routine, conventional activity is normally not sufficient to transform the law into patent-eligible subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption / prohibition on claims that wholly preempt natural correlations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that 'wholly preempt' a natural correlation or phenomenon — i.e., that cover every practical application of that natural law — are invalid under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The District Court held that Prometheus's claims 'wholly preempt' the correlations between metabolites and therapeutic efficacy, which led to rejection under §101. The concept of preemption is central: claims cannot be allowed to monopolize the basic tools of scientific and technological work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test as an important clue (but not dispositive)
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine-or-transformation test (a process is patent-eligible if tied to a particular machine or effects a transformation) is a valuable clue to patentability but is not an absolute rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit relied on the machine-or-transformation test to find the claim patentable (treating administration and measuring as transformative). The Supreme Court (in Bilski and via subsequent commentary in Mayo) characterized the test as an 'important clue' rather than the sole test for §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-as-a-whole analysis vs. isolating limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: One view (articulated by the Federal Circuit) is that patent eligibility should be assessed by considering the claim as a whole rather than isolating individual limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit stated: 'it is inappropriate to determine the patent eligibility of a claim as a whole based on whether selected limitations constitute patent-eligible subject matter.' This supports evaluating the combination of steps/limitations together when assessing §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental-step / data-gathering exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Purely mental steps or mere data-gathering activities are not patentable subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The District Court characterized the claims' first two steps as 'data-gathering' and the third step as a merely 'unpatentable mental step' (the correlation/decision). The court saw no required change in administered dose in the claimed steps, rendering the novel part effectively mental/informational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical transformation / concrete-step support for eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical transformations or concrete, technical steps (e.g., administering a drug to a patient, performing measurements) can weigh in favor of patent eligibility under tests like machine-or-transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit found the steps of administering the drug (transforming the patient) and measuring metabolites (concrete laboratory steps) to be transformative, supporting patentability. Mayo discusses this view even though the Supreme Court ultimately rejected Prometheus's claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity does not make a claim patent-eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: If the steps that apply a law of nature merely instruct practitioners to engage in well-understood, routine, conventional activity, those steps generally do not make the claim patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court: 'Because methods for making such determinations were well known in the art, this step simply tells doctors to engage in well-understood, routine, conventional activity previously engaged in by scientists in the field. Such activity is normally not sufficient to transform an unpatentable law of nature into a patent-eligible application of such a law.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent harmonization and reliance on historic cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of §101 eligibility relies on harmonizing and applying prior precedents (e.g., O'Reilly v. Morse, Neilson v. Harford, Bilski, LabCorp, Alice), which frame limits on claiming natural laws or abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Mayo opinion and article reference earlier cases and note that the Court sought to align its treatment of patent-eligibility with historical precedents. The Court also expressed deference to Congress for crafting policy changes if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO examination guidance post-Mayo / administrative standards
rubrics_metrics.description: After Mayo, the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office issued preliminary and interim guidelines (later incorporated into the MPEP) for examiners on process claims that include a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or correlation as a limiting element or step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Wikipedia article notes USPTO preliminary guidelines (March 21, 2012), interim guidelines (July 3, 2012), and later guidance implementing Mayo/Alice incorporated into the MPEP (notably Sections 2103 through 2106.07(c)). Examiners are directed to apply the Mayo/Alice framework when assessing claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy balancing: access to critical scientific data vs. innovation incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy considerations inform the debate over patent-eligibility, balancing the need to keep critical scientific data available for patient care and research against incentives for investment and innovation in fields like personalized medicine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses to the decision emphasize competing policy goals: supporters argued Mayo prevents monopolization of bodily responses and preserves access for patient care, while critics warned that restricting patents could chill investment in diagnostics and personalized medicine. The Court acknowledged policy implications and referenced Congress's role in tailoring rules.
